title_zh: 有什么好担心的？（代班主持：Bloomberg News 记者 Max Abelson）
subtitle_zh: Matt Levine 与代班主持 Max Abelson 聊 Clippers 丑闻、DAT 套利维权与 Apollo 的激进溢价。

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios. Podcasts. Radio. News. Matt, Matt, Matt, Matt, Matt. That's the only thing I have to say.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios. Podcasts. Radio. News. Matt，Matt，Matt，Matt，Matt。我要说的就这些了。

turns.en: I always, like, wish that our relationship was like in Annie Hall where Alvy and his friend both call each other Max constantly. Because I called you and I'm like, Max. And you never reply, yes, Max.
turns.zh: 我一直希望我俩的关系能像《Annie Hall》里那样，Alvy 和他朋友老是互相喊对方 Max。因为我给你打电话，我就喊，Max。可你从来不回一句，在呢，Max。

turns.en: Oh, yeah, you want me to probably by my name?
turns.zh: 哦，行，你是想让我用我自己的名字来称呼你？

turns.en: Probably not. You put it like that now. Absolutely not.
turns.zh: 大概不行吧。你这么一说，那绝对不行。

turns.en: So, Max.
turns.zh: 那就，Max。

turns.en: I've never... Mastered the intro of the guest hosts, but here we are.
turns.zh: 我一直没……没掌握好怎么介绍代班主持，不过既然都到这儿了。

turns.en: I'm a guest host.
turns.zh: 我是代班主持。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to the Money Stuff podcast, your weekly podcast where we talk about stuff related to money. I'm Matt Levine and I write the Money Stuff column for Bloomberg Opinion.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎来到 Money Stuff 播客，这是我们的每周一更节目，聊聊跟钱有关的那些事儿。我是 Matt Levine，我为 Bloomberg Opinion 写 Money Stuff 专栏。

turns.en: And I'm Max Abelson, a senior reporter here at Bloomberg News, where I write about money and power.
turns.zh: 我是 Max Abelson，Bloomberg News 的资深记者，我写的是关于金钱和权力（money and power）的报道。

turns.en: Money and power.
turns.zh: 金钱和权力。

turns.en: Yeah, you know, Matt only writes about money stuff. I write about money and power.
turns.zh: 对，你知道的，Matt 只写钱的那些事儿（money stuff）。我写的是金钱和权力。

turns.en: I don't like power.
turns.zh: 我不喜欢权力。

turns.en: I love power. I don't want it.
turns.zh: 我爱权力。但我并不想拥有它。

turns.en: No, I find power off-putting, and I enjoy money.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得权力让人反感，而我享受的是钱。

turns.en: You hold your nose once a subject crosses over from money to power. You're like, nope, can't put this in the column. It's about money, but it's also about power, so you've got to cross it off the list.
turns.zh: 一旦一个话题从钱跨到权力那边，你就捏着鼻子嫌弃了。你会说，不行，这个不能写进专栏。它是关于钱的，但也是关于权力的，所以你只能把它从清单上划掉。

turns.en: I sometimes quote Samuel Johnson, who says something like, man is seldom so innocently engaged as in the pursuit of money, as in getting money. He says, I know you disagree, but many people disagree. Many people think money is the roots of evils and things like that. But no, I think money is a charming and innocent subject and power is nefarious.
turns.zh: 我有时会引用 Samuel Johnson 的话，他大意是说，人很少有什么时候比追求金钱、比赚钱时更清白无邪了。他说……我知道你不同意，但很多人都不认同。很多人觉得金钱是万恶之源之类的。但不，我觉得钱是个迷人又清白的话题，而权力才是邪恶的。

turns.en: Well, speaking of charming and innocent, that's not the first time you've quoted Samuel Johnson at me.
turns.zh: 嗯，说到迷人又清白，这可不是你头一回冲我引用 Samuel Johnson 了。

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: Because I believe there's the... I do it a lot. There's the guy who's been seen going around shooting cats.
turns.zh: 因为我想有那么一段……我引用得很多。说的是有个人被看见四处去射杀猫。

turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，对。

turns.en: But that won't happen to my cat.
turns.zh: 但这事不会落到我那只猫身上。

turns.en: But Hodge shall not be shot. No, no, Hodge shall not be shot. No, that's in Life of Johnson, but.
turns.zh: 可 Hodge 绝不能被射杀。不不，Hodge 绝不能被射杀。不，这句是出自《Life of Johnson》，不过……

turns.en: It's... Pellfire.
turns.zh: 是……Pellfire。

turns.en: It's also the epigraph of Pellfire.
turns.zh: 它也是 Pellfire 的题词（epigraph）。

turns.en: Pellfire stuff.
turns.zh: Pellfire 那些事儿。

turns.en: Really, really, really... Setting a certain tone. She's talking about the Clippers.
turns.zh: 真的，真的，真的……算是定了个基调。她在讲 Clippers。

turns.en: Oh, there are a few things I'd rather talk about. It's so delicious. Go Knicks, first of all.
turns.zh: 哦，有几件事我更愿意聊。这太有意思了。首先，Go Knicks（尼克斯加油）。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Max is interested. So last week, the Clippers got in trouble with the NBA for paying Kawhi Leonard like millions of dollars under the table, basically, is the summary. And Max's interest in the story is twofold. One, he's a Knicks fan. And two, he's a fan of the dance that Steve Ballmer did on stage at a Microsoft event years ago, which is like truly one of the most.
turns.zh: 对，对。Max 很感兴趣。上周，Clippers 因为私下里给 Kawhi Leonard 塞了好几百万美元，惹上了 NBA 的麻烦，这基本就是整件事的概括。而 Max 对这条新闻的兴趣有两方面。一是他是 Knicks 的球迷。二是他很迷 Steve Ballmer 多年前在一场 Microsoft 活动上台跳的那段舞，那真是最……

turns.en: It's stunning.
turns.zh: 太惊艳了。

turns.en: Amazing videos.
turns.zh: 最牛的视频之一。

turns.en: You don't get to see a human being move their body just in the way Steve Ballmer moves his body. I think they're celebrating Windows 95.
turns.zh: 你可看不到别人能像 Steve Ballmer 那样活动自己的身体。我记得他们当时是在庆祝 Windows 95。

turns.en: That's true. Anyway, yeah. So the Clippers. So about a year ago, Pablo Torre broke the news that like the Clippers had this very weird deal with this thing. this fraudulent company called Aspiration Partners, where the Clippers were paying Aspiration millions of dollars for sort of vague environmental services. And Aspiration was paying Kawhi Leonard, it turns out, basically the same number of millions of dollars for an endorsement deal in which Kawhi Leonard did very, very little. And Poplitaria's thesis, which at the time was like surprising and controversial and just turns out to be just clearly true, although the Clippers still deny it. But the thesis was that this was a way for the Clippers to pay Kawhi Leonard, who's their star player, more than the NBA maximum contract amount. So they were like trying to, you know, they're recruiting star players. And the way to do that is, you know, there's a salary cap. You couldn't pay them more than a certain amount, but they could pay them millions of dollars more if they funneled that money in a like deniable way through Aspiration Partners. And so it does seem like they paid Aspiration Partners millions of dollars for possibly fake tree planting. And then Aspiration turned around and paid that same amount of money to Kawhi Leonard. for probably fake endorsement deals. And in this way, the Clippers were able to retain his services. And the NBA hired my old law firm, Wachtell Lifton, to do an investigation of this. And last week, they put out their report, and it's real bad for the Clippers. It basically confirms Paul Latorre's reporting and also finds a bunch of other endorsement deals that seem to have been both created and funded by the Clippers. Like the Clippers would pay companies millions of dollars of consulting fees, like to companies that were not consultants. And then the consulting fees would somehow find their way to Kawhi Leonard.
turns.zh: 没错。总之，是啊，说说 Clippers。大约一年前，Pablo Torre 爆料说，Clippers 跟一家……一家叫 Aspiration Partners 的欺诈公司有一笔很古怪的交易，Clippers 付给 Aspiration 好几百万美元，买一些含含糊糊的环保服务。结果发现，Aspiration 又付给 Kawhi Leonard 基本同样数额的几百万美元，作为一份代言合约，而 Kawhi Leonard 在这份代言里几乎什么都没做。Pablo Torre 的论点，当时听起来很出人意料、很有争议，结果却被证明明摆着是真的，尽管 Clippers 到现在还否认。他的论点是：这是 Clippers 给他们的球星 Kawhi Leonard 支付超过 NBA 顶薪合同上限的一种办法。他们当时是在招募球星嘛。而办法就是，你知道，有个工资帽（salary cap）。你不能付给球员超过某个额度，但如果他们把这笔钱通过 Aspiration Partners 以一种可以抵赖的方式转出去，就能多付几百万美元。所以看起来，他们确实付了 Aspiration Partners 几百万美元，买可能是假的植树服务。然后 Aspiration 转手又把同样数额的钱付给 Kawhi Leonard，买可能是假的代言合约。就这样，Clippers 得以留住他的服务。NBA 请了我以前所在的律所 Wachtell Lipton 来做一项调查。上周他们发布了报告，对 Clippers 非常不利。它基本上证实了 Pablo Torre 的报道，还发现了一堆别的代言合约，看起来既是由 Clippers 撮合、又是由 Clippers 出资的。比如 Clippers 会给一些公司付几百万美元的咨询费，而这些公司根本不是做咨询的。然后这些咨询费又会不知怎么地流到 Kawhi Leonard 那里。

turns.en: It was like the stadium display maker, basically, right?
turns.zh: 基本上就是那个做球场显示屏的公司，对吧？

turns.en: Oh yeah, they paid consulting fees. I forget what the other few companies, they were like companies that didn't do consulting, but they also paid consulting fees to the people who did the scoreboard in the stadium. And then they also called the scoreboard company and they were like, we would like to increase the price that we're paying for the scoreboard. And by the way, We're expecting you to turn around and spend that money on Kawhi Leonard.
turns.zh: 哦对，他们付了咨询费。另外几家公司我记不清了，反正都是些不做咨询的公司，但他们也给做球场记分牌的人付了咨询费。然后他们还打电话给那家记分牌公司说，我们想提高我们买记分牌付的价钱。顺便说一句，我们指望你们转手把这笔钱花在 Kawhi Leonard 身上。

turns.en: It's a splendid scandal. I mean, it's got novelistic qualities. I mean, I think Aspiration, right, that's the main one. Yeah.
turns.zh: 这是一桩精彩的丑闻。我是说，它有小说般的质感。我觉得 Aspiration，对吧，那是主要的一家。是的。

turns.en: I don't even know if that's the main one. It's the one that sort of broke up in the story. And it's the craziest one because they were, like, the guy who founded that company and did this deal with, you know, the club versus Kawhi Leonard is now in prison.
turns.zh: 我都不确定那是不是主要的一家。它是那个最先在报道里爆出来的。而且它是最疯狂的一家，因为，你知道，创立那家公司、跟俱乐部、跟 Kawhi Leonard 做这笔交易的那个人，现在已经进监狱了。

turns.en: Sandberg, I think.
turns.zh: 叫 Sandberg，我记得。

turns.en: Yeah, Joe Sandberg is his name. And the company is crazy. And, like, before they all collapsed, like, I think in 2024, Aspiration was, like, gearing up for an IPO. And it was, like, a kind of vague tree-planting environment. It's like an environment. There's, like, a debit card that somehow gave you environmental credits. It was, like, sort of, like, consumer-facing environmental whatever. But to, like, juice their revenue, apparently, there's, like, a 2024 Bloomberg Green investigation. To juice their revenue, Aspiration would do these, like, round-trip deals where They would find customers who, for some reason, were usually Colombian celebrities, like actors or soccer players from Colombia. And they would pay these customers, write deals where these customers would agree to pay them tens of thousands of dollars to plant trees. And the tree planting was like, someone else was planting the trees and they were reselling the tree planting at high markups, which is an absurd business to be in. But they would get tens of thousands of dollars of revenue for tree planting. And then Joe Sandberg's other company would turn around and pay the same amount of money to these Colombian celebrities for like marketing deals. So no money would change hands. The Colombian celebrities would never pay or receive anything, but they just like sign their name on a piece of paper. And for that aspiration could book revenues, which got them in trouble. But so like when Pablo Torre broke the story, I was like, this is a company that is in the business of doing fake endorsement deals for like reasons of their own. And so, like, you know, and the Clippers are like, hey, could we do a fake endorsement? It's like, perfect, yes. Give us some fake revenue. We'll do some fake endorsement deals. It's like the business model.
turns.zh: 对，他叫 Joe Sandberg。这家公司很疯狂。在他们彻底垮掉之前，我记得是 2024 年，Aspiration 还在筹备 IPO。它做的是那种含含糊糊的植树环保……就是环保那一挂。有一张借记卡，不知怎么就能给你环保积分。就是那种面向消费者的环保什么的。但为了给营收注水，显然——有一篇 2024 年 Bloomberg Green 的调查报道——为了给营收注水，Aspiration 会做这种来回倒账（round-trip）的交易：他们会找一些客户，不知为何这些客户通常是哥伦比亚的名人，比如哥伦比亚的演员或足球运动员。他们会给这些客户……签一些合约，让这些客户同意付给他们几万美元去植树。而植树这件事呢，其实是别人在种树，他们只是把植树服务加价高卖出去，这本身就是个荒唐的生意。但他们能靠植树拿到几万美元的营收。然后 Joe Sandberg 的另一家公司又转手把同样数额的钱付给这些哥伦比亚名人，作为所谓的营销合约。所以根本没有钱真正易手。这些哥伦比亚名人从没付过、也没收过任何东西，他们只是在一张纸上签个名。就凭这个，Aspiration 就能确认营收（book revenues），这也让他们惹上了麻烦。所以当 Pablo Torre 爆出这条新闻时，我就想，这本来就是一家干假代言生意、出于自己目的的公司。于是 Clippers 说，嘿，我们能做个假代言吗？对方就说，太好了，可以啊。给我们弄点假营收，我们就做点假代言。这简直就是它们的商业模式。

turns.en: It's like, you know, scandals come and go. Any idiot can have a little scandal. But a scandal on top of a scandal, you know?
turns.zh: 就是说，你知道，丑闻来了又走。任何蠢货都能闹出点小丑闻。但丑闻之上再叠一桩丑闻，你懂吧？

turns.en: Right. It's like, I truly don't know what was going on. Like, I think some people at Aspiration were, and you see this in the Wachtell report, like some people at Aspiration were like, why are we paying Kawhi Leonard this much money? He's not like a big endorser. He's not doing anything for us. Why are we doing this? And Joe Sanra's like, ah, we'll get it all back.
turns.zh: 对。就是说，我真的搞不懂当时到底怎么回事。我觉得 Aspiration 内部有些人——你在 Wachtell 报告里能看到——有些人就问，我们为什么要付给 Kawhi Leonard 这么多钱？他又不是什么大牌代言人。他也没为我们做什么。我们为什么要这么干？而 Joe Sandberg 就说，啊，我们都会赚回来的。

turns.en: Trust me.
turns.zh: 相信我。

turns.en: But, like, you get the sense that Aspiration was, like, kind of a big company, and some people involved in it were not simply there to do fraud, but, like, the whole thing was kind of doing a lot of fraud.
turns.zh: 但你会感觉到，Aspiration 算是家挺大的公司，里面有些人并不是单纯来搞欺诈的，可整家公司却在干着大量欺诈的勾当。

turns.en: Shout out to Pablo and his staff. That's good reporting. But also, you know what? Credit goes to Wachtel, your former bosses. I feel like, Matt, in my mind's eye, this is probably... very, very wrong. You'll be disappointed with me for having thought this. But in my mind's eye, I thought that when you go to like an external law firm to, you know, do an independent review, I always like a part of me, like imagine that was a way of like trying to get something like a clean bill of health in public after, you know, the scare of a scandal. And then the Wachtell report comes out. It's like, it's worse. It made this look like a bigger scandal, not a smaller scandal. I was kind of amazed. I was sort of impressed, but maybe that's not fair to law firms in their reviews.
turns.zh: 向 Pablo 和他的团队致敬。那是很棒的报道。不过，你知道吗？功劳也归于 Wachtell，你的老东家。我觉得，Matt，在我脑海里，这个想法很可能……非常非常错。你会因为我这么想过而对我失望。但在我脑海里，我一直以为，当你去找一家外部律所来做独立审查时，我心里总有一部分觉得，那是一种想在丑闻惊魂之后、公开拿到一份'清白无恙'证明（clean bill of health）的手段。可结果 Wachtell 的报告出来了。它是说，情况更糟。它让这件事看起来是一桩更大的丑闻，而不是更小的。我有点吃惊。我也有点佩服，但也许这么想对律所做的那些审查不太公平。

turns.en: No, I think the proper cynical interpretation of law firm outside investigations is that they are designed to throw someone under the bus who is probably not the person writing the check to the law firm, right? So in many internal investigations, the upshot is this one bad apple did some real bad stuff. A classic law firm internal investigation is conducted in the shadow of some sort of Regulatory investigation or like justice department investigation. And often the purpose, the deep purpose of the law firm investigation is to get the justice department not to charge the company with something bad. And often the way to do that is to serve up some sacrificial victims to the justice department and be like, this is the guy who did the crime and here's all the evidence against them. So charge him. And then like the company gets credit for cooperating. And so, you know, you're right that the point of a law firm investigation is to make, is often to make the company look good. But often the way to do that is to make some selected person look as bad as possible. That's not what's going on here because, like, first of all, there's probably no, like, you know, this is just, like, a scandal. It's not like the Justice Department is going to shut down the NBA. And secondly, like, it's not clear what the NBA's incentives are here. Like, maybe it would be better for the NBA to be like, nope, nothing wrong here. But they do seem to have given Wachtell free reign and Wachtell seems to have had a lot of fun. And, like, you know, they found a lot of bad stuff. Allegedly. I mean, like, you know, the Clippers still say this was a biased investigation and everything was fine. But it's like it's really like they find these consulting fees and then they go interview the people at the companies who say, well, we don't do any consulting. And we thought it was pretty weird to get these consulting fees and they paid them all up front. And so there's a lot of bad stuff.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得对律所外部调查，正确的犬儒式解读是：它们的设计初衷，就是把某个大概率不是给律所开支票的那个人推出去背锅，对吧？所以在很多内部调查里，结论都是'就是这一颗坏苹果干了很坏的事'。一场经典的律所内部调查，往往是在某种监管调查、或者司法部（Justice Department）调查的阴影下进行的。而律所调查的深层目的，常常是让司法部别对公司提起什么严重的指控。而做到这一点的常见方式，就是给司法部献上几个替罪羊，然后说，这个人才是犯罪的那个，这是对他不利的全部证据，所以起诉他吧。这样公司就能因'配合调查'而得到好评。所以你说得对，律所调查的目的常常是让公司好看。但让公司好看的常见方式，往往是让某个被挑出来的人尽可能难看。而这次的情况不是这样，因为，首先，这大概率就是……一桩丑闻而已。司法部又不会去关停 NBA。其次，NBA 在这里的动机也不清楚。也许对 NBA 来说更好的说法是'不，这里什么问题都没有'。但他们似乎确实放开了手让 Wachtell 去查，而 Wachtell 似乎查得很开心。他们发现了很多糟糕的东西。据称如此。我是说，Clippers 至今还说这是一场有偏见的调查、一切都好。但实际情况是，他们真的发现了这些咨询费，然后去采访那些公司的人，对方说，我们根本不做咨询，收到这些咨询费我们觉得挺奇怪，而且他们还是一次性全额预付的。所以确实有很多糟糕的东西。

turns.en: I will say I was watching live on Kawhi Leonard hit. I mean, this was for a different basketball. This is for the Raptors. The coolest shot I've ever seen.
turns.zh: 我得说，我是亲眼看直播看着 Kawhi Leonard 投进那球的。我是说，那是为另一支球队投的，是为 Raptors（猛龙）投的。那是我见过的最酷的一投。

turns.en: Yeah. The Clippers got him right after that, right?
turns.zh: 对。Clippers 就是在那之后马上签下他的，对吧？

turns.en: I think right after that. I think he left the Raptors. I mean, that was in the Eastern Conference semifinals. Probably the first time the Eastern Conference semifinals have been mentioned on a podcast. But it was awesome.
turns.zh: 我记得就是那之后。他好像就是那时候离开 Raptors 的。那是在东部半决赛（Eastern Conference semifinals）里。这可能是东部半决赛头一回在播客里被提到。但那球太棒了。

turns.en: Is that true? You talk a lot about sports betting, but you're probably not a lot about individual games.
turns.zh: 真的吗？你经常聊体育博彩（sports betting），但你大概不怎么聊单场比赛。

turns.en: It was sick.
turns.zh: 那球太炸了。

turns.en: Sick.
turns.zh: 炸裂。

turns.en: And so was the lockdown. Report. I want to talk about a phrase I wouldn't have known if it weren't for you. Empory Digital.
turns.zh: 还有那份报告也一样炸。我想聊一个词，要不是因为你，我根本不会知道。Empery Digital。

turns.en: Oh, man.
turns.zh: 哦，天呐。

turns.en: Empory Digital. What a great, great word.
turns.zh: Empery Digital。多棒、多棒的一个词啊。

turns.en: Empory Digital is a dat.
turns.zh: Empery Digital 是一家 DAT（digital asset treasury，数字资产财库公司）。

turns.en: Do you know what a dat is? Tell me what a dat is.
turns.zh: 你知道 DAT 是什么吗？跟我说说 DAT 是什么。

turns.en: So, Empory Digital is like an electric motorcycle company in the not very distant past. But in 2025, a thing that small public companies could do was they could just get a big stash of Bitcoin. And then, you know, if they had $ 100 million of Bitcoin, their stock would trade at like a $ 200 million valuation. And this is a great trade for people who had stashes of Bitcoin. And so Empory Digital, like, you know, dozens of other smallish public companies pivoted to being a digital asset treasury company, as they call it, a DAT. So it got like, I don't know, $ 500 million of Bitcoin. And it was like, ooh, look, we traded a premium. We're going to be the future of holding Bitcoin or whatever. They did this in like July of 2025. It's really like the peak of the popularity of this trade. And soon after that, the trade stopped working because there's never any reason that these stocks would trade at a premium to the Bitcoin. It's just like a thing that people got really into for a while. And so it stopped working and they stopped trading at premiums and often started trading at discounts to the value of their Bitcoin. And when that happened, you know, the point of the DAT was like, if you had a stash of Bitcoin, those were the $ 100 million, you could sell it for $ 100 million. But if you plopped it into a DAT, then you'd have $ 200 million worth of stock and you sell that for $ 200 million and you'd have more money, right? So it's a great trade, Because you could turn $ 1 of Bitcoin into $ 2 of stock. But when it reversed and these DATs were trading at a discount, people realized that you could turn $ 0. 90 of stock into $ 1 of Bitcoin. Because what you do is buy up a DAT and then crack it open, sell all the Bitcoin, and it would sell for more than the value of the stock that you bought. So people started, I mean, not that many people. The idea of DAT activism became a thing.
turns.zh: Empery Digital 在不算久远的过去是一家电动摩托车公司。但在 2025 年，小型上市公司能做的一件事，就是直接囤一大堆比特币（Bitcoin）。然后，你知道，如果他们手里有 1 亿美元的比特币，他们的股票就能以大约 2 亿美元的估值交易。对那些囤着比特币的人来说，这是笔很棒的交易。所以 Empery Digital，跟其他几十家规模不大的上市公司一样，转型成了所谓的数字资产财库公司（digital asset treasury company），也就是 DAT。于是它弄到了大概，我不知道，5 亿美元的比特币。然后就说，ooh，看，我们有溢价交易。我们要成为持有比特币的未来之类的。他们是在 2025 年 7 月左右这么做的，那正好是这类交易最火的高峰。可没多久，这交易就不灵了，因为这些股票根本没有理由相对比特币存在溢价。它只是人们一度很上头的东西。于是它不灵了，这些股票不再以溢价交易，反而常常开始相对其比特币的价值折价交易。而当这种情况发生时，DAT 的意义本来是：如果你有一堆比特币，值 1 亿美元，你可以按 1 亿美元卖掉。但如果你把它塞进一家 DAT，那你就有了价值 2 亿美元的股票，你能按 2 亿美元卖掉，钱就更多了，对吧？所以这是笔很棒的交易，因为你能把 1 美元的比特币变成 2 美元的股票。可当它反转、这些 DAT 开始折价交易时，人们意识到，你能把 0.90 美元的股票变成 1 美元的比特币。因为你要做的，就是买下一家 DAT，然后把它拆开，卖掉所有比特币，卖出的钱会比你买股票花的钱更多。于是人们开始……我是说，没多少人。DAT 维权（DAT activism）这个概念就成了一种风潮。

turns.en: DAT activism?
turns.zh: DAT 维权？

turns.en: Because you could buy stock in a DAT and then yell at the board and say, you should sell the Bitcoin and liquidate the company, and you'll sell the Bitcoin for more than the value of the stock because it's trading at a discount. This was complicated by the fact that M3 Digital, in 2025, they went from being an electric motorcycle company to being a DAT. In 2026, they went from being a DAT to being an AI infrastructure company because that's The 2026 trade. I think they're no longer trading at a discount. But anyway, they were doing some Bitcoin buybacks. They were kind of doing some version of this trade. And then some activists got into the stock and were like, we're going to crack this open. And two of the activists are a guy named Gabby Glicksberg, who runs a fund called ATG, and another guy named Tice Brown. There's like a lawsuit over their data activism. And in the lawsuit, the judge, in the judicial opinion. He quotes an email that Tice sent to me being like, I forget what he said, but he said something like, I want to do activism at a dat. And I was like, I was like, yes.
turns.zh: 因为你可以买一家 DAT 的股票，然后冲着董事会喊：你们应该把比特币卖掉、把公司清算了，你们卖比特币拿到的钱会比股票的价值更多，因为它现在是折价交易的。这件事又因为 Empery Digital 的情况变得更复杂：2025 年，它从一家电动摩托车公司变成了 DAT；2026 年，它又从 DAT 变成了一家 AI 基础设施公司，因为那是 2026 年的热门交易。我想它现在已经不再折价交易了。总之，他们当时在做一些比特币回购，算是某种版本的这类操作。然后一些维权投资者（activists）买进了这只股票，说我们要把它拆开。其中两个维权者，一个叫 Gabby Glicksberg，管理着一只叫 ATG 的基金，另一个叫 Tice Brown。围绕他们的 DAT 维权有一场官司。在这场官司里，法官在司法意见书中，引用了一封 Tice 发给我的邮件，我忘了他具体怎么说，但大意是，我想在一家 DAT 搞维权。而我当时的反应就是，好啊。

turns.en: You know, that's so interesting.
turns.zh: 你知道，这太有意思了。

turns.en: I was like, my eyes lit up, you know.
turns.zh: 我当时就，眼睛都亮了，你知道。

turns.en: You've asked me, I think several times, offensively so, why anyone would be willing to talk to me. I hope you mean journalistically, not like, you know, personally. You've wondered why is it that people are willing to go on the record when that could, you know.
turns.zh: 你问过我，我想有好几次，还挺冒犯的，为什么会有人愿意跟我聊。我希望你说的是新闻采访意义上的，而不是，你知道，私人意义上的。你一直纳闷，为什么人们愿意实名公开发言（go on the record），哪怕那可能会，你知道。

turns.en: You do a number of things, but One thing you do is you write about money and power and you, how can I put this? You allow rich and powerful people to make fools of themselves or to express their innermost selves, which are bad.
turns.zh: 你做了很多事，但其中一件是，你写金钱和权力，而且你，怎么说呢？你让那些有钱有势的人出洋相，或者让他们流露出最内心的自我，而那个自我是很糟的。

turns.en: Well, I don't think they would see it that way. Apparently not. But let me just say honestly, like honest to goodness, I'm not so sure. I don't think I see it that way either. You know, it's like, why am I talking to a microphone across from you? You know, I'm probably, definitely will sound not as smart as you.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得他们不会这么看。显然不会。但让我老实说，说真心话，我也不太确定。我也不觉得自己是这么看的。你知道，就像，我为什么对着你、对着麦克风在这儿说话？我很可能、肯定是听起来没你聪明。

turns.en: Yeah, no, we're definitely both making fools of ourselves.
turns.zh: 是啊，不，我俩肯定都在出洋相。

turns.en: But yet people do want the chance to kind of explain themselves and give an accounting of what they've been up to. And I actually, I remember what he said. I put it down and I loved it. I'd like to liquidate a Bitcoin treasury company. I'd like to speak publicly about it. And that cracks me up because it's like, it really goes to show. It's like whatever people are up to, they might be up to liquidating a Bitcoin treasury company. They do want to speak publicly about it. Not all the time, but some people want to talk about it some of the times and bless them for wanting to talk to you about it or me.
turns.zh: 但人们确实想要一个机会，来解释自己、来交代他们一直在干什么。而且我其实还记得他说的话。我把它记下来了，我很喜欢。他说：'我想清算一家比特币财库公司。我想公开谈谈这件事。'这话把我逗乐了，因为它真的说明问题。就像，不管人们在忙什么——他们可能正忙着清算一家比特币财库公司——他们确实想公开谈这件事。不是任何时候都想，但有些人有些时候是想谈的，为他们愿意跟你、或者跟我聊这件事而祝福他们吧。

turns.en: And by the way, that email to me is quoted in the judicial opinion. And then like the day after he sent that email, I published a column about like the going on at Empory, which I think I mentioned it, but I don't think I, maybe I quoted a filing. I think he sent letters. So I quoted, but like, it's not like, it's not like he did speak publicly through me. It's not like he gave me an extensive interview in which I quoted him. Right. I mean, like I just wrote about it.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，他发给我的那封邮件被引用进了司法意见书里。然后，就在他发出那封邮件的第二天，我发表了一篇专栏，讲 Empery 那边发生的事，我想我提到了它，但我不确定，也许我引用了一份文件。我想他发了一些信函。所以我引用了，但这不是说，不是说他真的通过我公开发了言。也不是说他接受了我一次详尽的采访、让我引用他的话。对吧。我是说，我只是把这事写了出来。

turns.en: Well, I can say the very same. I mean, people talk on the record, but they talk on background.
turns.zh: 嗯，我也完全可以说同样的话。我是说，人们会实名公开发言，但也会以背景消息（on background）的方式发言。

turns.en: But I do think that when people email me, sometimes it's because they're like, I want to say my two cents about whatever, and then I often ignore them. But sometimes it's like, I would like to liquidate a dat. And they know that my eyes will light up at that sentence, because that's a funny sentence. Not to everyone, but to me. I find that a very funny sentence. Like, as soon as I got that email, I was like, oh, why have I not thought of this? Why has no one done this? Why is this not a thing? And, like, it's a little bit of a thing now.
turns.zh: 但我确实觉得，人们给我发邮件时，有时候是因为他们想说，我想对某件事发表点愚见（my two cents），这种我通常就忽略了。但有时候是这种：我想清算一家 DAT。他们知道，我一看到这句话眼睛就会亮起来，因为那是句很有意思的话。不是对所有人都这样，但对我是。我觉得那是句非常好笑的话。就像，我一收到那封邮件就想，哦，我怎么没想到这个？怎么没人做过这个？这怎么还没成为一种玩法？而现在，它多少算是成为一种玩法了。

turns.en: You love the rules of the game.
turns.zh: 你热爱这套游戏规则。

turns.en: Well.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: You like knowing what the rules are, and I guess very, very highly paid people in finance also do that so that they can then profit from it. You like knowing the rules so that you can then explain it in a very humorous manner.
turns.zh: 你喜欢搞清楚规则是什么，我猜金融圈那些收入非常非常高的人也是这么做的，好让他们从中获利。而你喜欢搞清规则，是为了能用非常幽默的方式把它讲出来。

turns.en: So that I can delight in them, right? And, by the way, I think that, like, this is, like, an underappreciated thing about the financial industry, like, When I was a derivative structure at a bank, was I getting paid well? I was getting paid okay. But I wasn't doing the derivative structuring purely because there was a pot of money at the end of it. I was doing it because it was quite lovely.
turns.zh: 好让我乐在其中，对吧？而且，顺便说一句，我觉得这是金融行业里一个被低估的特点。我在银行做衍生品结构化（derivative structuring）那会儿，我薪水高吗？还算过得去。但我做衍生品结构化，并不纯粹是因为终点有一大笔钱。我做它，是因为它相当美妙。

turns.en: For the love of the game. Yes.
turns.zh: 出于对这场游戏的热爱。是的。

turns.en: Both during and after working at a bank, I was like, this derivative structuring is so beautiful. And now I get to just convey the aesthetic appreciation of finance without the long hours. But part of the thesis of the column is that I am not the only one with an aesthetic appreciation of the finer points of finance. And I think a lot of people who do it for a living also have an aesthetic appreciation for it. And I think Thijs Brand might be one of those people.
turns.zh: 在银行工作期间和之后，我一直觉得，这种衍生品结构化太美了。而现在，我可以只传递对金融的那种审美欣赏，却不用熬那些长时间的班。但这个专栏的部分论点就是：并不是只有我一个人对金融的精妙之处有审美上的欣赏。我觉得很多以此为生的人，对它也有审美上的欣赏。而我觉得 Tice Brown 可能就是那样的人之一。

turns.en: Finance is delightful.
turns.zh: 金融很迷人。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: What are you going to say? That's just great.
turns.zh: 你还能说什么呢？那真是太棒了。

turns.en: I mean, the other thing about the story is that basically, like, Gabby Glicksberg, one of the activists at Empery, was running a proxy fight, tried to get his board nominees on the board so that, you know, basically he could liquidate the data and capture the discounts. and um the current board was like no you can't do that your directors are ineligible for various reasons and so there's a lawsuit and like the delaware court basically ruled in favor of gabby glicksburg and was like you can run your guys for election although like there was a ruling basically basically every concern that the company had the court was like yeah that's fair like like there was like some like communications between gabby glicksburg and tice brown that maybe shouldn't have been and like weren't preserved and the judge sympathized with their concerns and like actually sanctioned the other side, but like did say the main thing is you can run your guys for election.
turns.zh: 我是说，这件事的另一点是，基本上，Empery 的维权者之一 Gabby Glicksberg 当时在打一场代理权之争（proxy fight），想把他提名的董事送进董事会，这样他基本就能清算这家 DAT、吃掉那个折价。而现任董事会说，不行，你不能这么干，你提名的人因为各种原因不具备资格。于是就有了一场官司。Delaware 法院基本上判 Gabby Glicksberg 胜诉，说你可以推你的人参加选举——尽管有一项裁决……基本上公司提出的每一点担忧，法院都说，嗯，这有道理，比如 Gabby Glicksberg 和 Tice Brown 之间有一些也许本不该发生、而且没有被保存下来的通信，法官对他们的担忧表示理解，甚至还制裁了对方，但确实说了，核心的一点是：你可以推你的人参加选举。

turns.en: Correct me if I'm wrong. The central question at hand was like had to do with hedging.
turns.zh: 我说错了你纠正我。当时核心的那个问题，好像跟对冲（hedging）有关。

turns.en: Well, there's two questions. One is like the communication, right? We're basically like, there's like two or three guys who are activists. And like the question is, are they a group? And if they're a group, did they disclose that accurately? And like, you know, the company's like, yeah, they didn't disclose it. And basically the judge was like, you have to let them run anyway, even if they're, some valid concerns about whether they were coordinating. But then the other question, which I thought was just more interesting, I don't know if it's the main question, but it's a more interesting question is like the trade here is you buy a dollar worth of Bitcoin in a debt for 90 cents because like it's trading at a discount, but then you're long Bitcoin, right? And like, you don't want to be long Bitcoin. You just want to capture that discount. And so you sell a dollar worth of Bitcoin in like the Bitcoin market. And so in fact, the activists here had some sort of Bitcoin hedge where basically they're like Delta neutral Bitcoin, right? Like they're, they're long the debt and they're short, like the proportion of underlying Bitcoin. And the company was like, they have to disclose that. And like, that's really bad. And so they shouldn't be eligible to run because their interests are not aligned with those of shareholders because every other shareholder in this debt. In theory, it's like long a pot of Bitcoin because that's what the debt is. And these guys are not long a pot of Bitcoin. They're they're neutral to Bitcoin. And they're just in it to crack open the DAT and capture the discount, which I think is a really interesting claim. And I think it's wrong, but it's just contingently wrong. It's just like, what is the DAT? If you believe that the DAT is a vehicle for true believers to hold Bitcoin, which I think is true of strategy, the original DAT, then it's like, yes, if you're not long Bitcoin, if you're hedging your Bitcoin, then you are not aligned with shareholders. But I think most DATs Like, just, like, the way they were formed, it's all, like, the shareholder base is all, like, the same, like, 12 hedge funds. It's very, like, it's very arbitrage-y. And so I think that, like, all of the shareholders in this data are kind of, like, there for the premium and, like, sad about the discount. And so, like, they are kind of aligned. But it's just, like, you know, I don't know. That's just my impression.
turns.zh: 嗯，有两个问题。一个是那些通信，对吧？基本上是，有两三个维权者。问题是，他们算不算一个'团体'（group）？如果算，他们有没有准确披露这一点？公司就说，是啊，他们没披露。而法官基本上说，你无论如何都得让他们参选，即便对于他们是否在协同行动确实有一些合理的疑虑。然后另一个问题，我觉得更有意思，我不知道它是不是主要问题，但更有意思：这里的交易是，你用 90 美分买到一家 DAT 里价值 1 美元的比特币，因为它在折价交易，但这样一来你就做多了比特币，对吧？而你并不想做多比特币。你只想吃掉那个折价。所以你在比特币市场上卖出价值 1 美元的比特币。因此事实上，这里的维权者做了某种比特币对冲，基本上他们对比特币是 Delta 中性（Delta neutral）的，对吧？就是他们做多这家 DAT，同时做空相应比例的底层比特币。公司就说，他们必须披露这一点，而且这很糟糕，所以他们不该有资格参选，因为他们的利益跟股东不一致——因为这家里其他每一个股东，理论上都是做多一堆比特币的，因为 DAT 本身就是这个。而这几个人并不做多比特币。他们对比特币是中性的。他们进来就是为了拆开这家 DAT、吃掉折价。我觉得这是个非常有意思的主张。而且我觉得它是错的，但只是'视情况而定'的错。就在于，这家 DAT 到底是什么？如果你相信 DAT 是供真正的信仰者持有比特币的工具——我觉得 Strategy（最初那家 DAT）就是这样——那么，是的，如果你不做多比特币、如果你在给你的比特币对冲，那你就跟股东利益不一致。但我觉得大多数 DAT，从它们成立的方式看，股东基础都是同样的那大概 12 家对冲基金。这非常有套利（arbitrage）味道。所以我觉得这家 DAT 里所有的股东，多少都是冲着溢价来的，又为折价而难过。所以他们的利益多少是一致的。但这只是，你知道，我不确定。这只是我的印象。

turns.en: Arbitrage is one of those words that when I started covering finance as a journalist, I thought was meaningless and fancy and people used it to sound smart, sort of like the equivalent of saying finance instead of finance. But I feel like, actually... Arbitrage is a very neat way of saying kind of what we're talking about, that there is something really delightful about understanding what's going on and trying to get a little premium, you know, coming or going.
turns.zh: 套利（arbitrage）是这么一种词：我刚开始当金融记者那会儿，觉得它空洞又花哨，人们用它来显摆自己聪明，就有点像用文绉绉的说法代替大白话。但我现在觉得，其实……套利是个很巧妙的词，正好形容我们在聊的这件事——搞懂到底在发生什么、再想办法赚一点溢价，无论买入还是卖出方向，这里头有种特别迷人的东西。

turns.en: Right. I think the arb is just like you can own a dat, you know, an empery or strategy or whatever, because you want to be long Bitcoin. That's the easiest way to be long Bitcoin. Or you can own. the DAT and be short Bitcoin and not have any Bitcoin exposure and be trading something else and the something else is like not you know risk-free but it's an arbitrage in the sense of your long and short like related instruments and you're trying to capture the difference between them and that's what's happening here right like the original that trade was like all these people are like i can buy bitcoin and plop it into a debt and like immediately double the value so that's an arbitrage right and like so when you could easily raise money for a debt by like you know going out to hedge funds and doing that trade and now that when that reverses and like when a dollar of bitcoin is worth 90 cents on a debt then like all the hedge funds are like well you know Do the trade the other way.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得这个套利就是：你可以持有一家 DAT，比如 Empery 或者 Strategy 之类的，因为你想做多比特币，那是做多比特币最简单的方式。或者，你也可以持有这家 DAT、同时做空比特币，不承担任何比特币敞口，而是在交易别的东西；而这个'别的东西'并不是无风险的，但它是一种套利，意思是你同时做多和做空相关的工具，试图吃掉它们之间的差价，这里发生的正是这个。最初那笔交易是，所有人都想，我可以买比特币、把它塞进一家 DAT，立刻让价值翻倍，这就是套利，对吧？所以当你能轻松地靠出去找对冲基金、做那笔交易来为一家 DAT 募资——而现在当它反转、当一家 DAT 里 1 美元的比特币只值 90 美分时，所有对冲基金就想，那好，那就把这笔交易反着做。

turns.en: It's a beautiful thing. I got to say arbitrage and finance.
turns.zh: 这真是一件美妙的事。我总算能说上一句套利和金融了。

turns.en: You did.
turns.zh: 你说了。

turns.en: My mother will think I'm so smart.
turns.zh: 我妈会觉得我特别聪明。

turns.en: So we're recording this on Wednesday. I wrote on Tuesday about this spat between Vlad Tenev and Adam Aaron. So Vlad Tenev is the CEO of Robinhood. Adam Aaron is the CEO of AMC Entertainment, the movie theater chain, and Memestock. And so Robinhood have gotten really into, like, tokenizing stocks, and they're doing this thing where they're offering, outside of America, they're offering a tokenized version of some public company stocks, including AMCs. And, like, Adam Aaron got wind of that and he got mad, and he, like, tweeted, like, this is, you know, this is fake stock or whatever. I forget what he said. You probably will actually know. And then, like, Vlad Danov's like, what's the problem here? And so they got in a little fight. And I wrote about it because, like, I think, like, they both have, like, reasonable opinions. Whereas, like, Adam Aaron, as the CEO of a meme stock, really wants to sort of control his shareholder base and, like, know where all the shares are. And Vlad Tenev, as the CEO of a, like, meme stock boutique, meme stock bazaar, maybe, wants to, like, you know, make his own, you know, variance on meme stocks. And so Robinhood is basically, like, you know, making, rolling its own AMC stock. And AMC doesn't like that.
turns.zh: 我们这是在周三录的。我周二写了一篇，讲 Vlad Tenev 和 Adam Aron 之间的这场口角。Vlad Tenev 是 Robinhood 的 CEO。Adam Aron 是 AMC Entertainment——那家院线连锁、也是只 meme 股——的 CEO。Robinhood 最近非常迷'把股票代币化'（tokenizing stocks）这件事，他们在做这样一个东西：在美国以外，他们提供某些上市公司股票的代币化版本，其中就包括 AMC 的。Adam Aron 听到风声后就火了，他发推说，这是，你知道，这是假股票之类的。我忘了他具体怎么说。你大概会知道。然后 Vlad Tenev 就说，这有什么问题？于是他俩就小小地吵了一架。我写这件事，是因为我觉得他俩的观点都挺有道理。Adam Aron 作为一只 meme 股的 CEO，很想掌控自己的股东基础、想知道所有的股票都在谁手里。而 Vlad Tenev 作为一家……meme 股精品店、或者说是 meme 股集市——的 CEO，想自己做出 meme 股的各种变体。所以 Robinhood 基本上就是在自己'攒'一种 AMC 股票。而 AMC 不喜欢这样。

turns.en: Nothing he said could possibly be funnier than the actual thing the other guy said was the quasi-fake market you're creating on the island of Jersey, which is a wonderful insult. And I said, what's the concern?
turns.zh: 他说的任何话，都不可能比对方那句原话更好笑——那句是：'你在 Jersey 岛上搞的这个准假冒市场（quasi-fake market）'，这可真是个精彩的讽刺。然后我就说，有什么好担心的？（what's the concern?）

turns.en: What's the concern?
turns.zh: 有什么好担心的？

turns.en: What's the concern?
turns.zh: 有什么好担心的？

turns.en: And, like, I don't know. I wrote this, like, there is a really powerful intuition, particularly at, like, meme stock companies for some reason, for good reason. There's this powerful intuition that, like, Only a company can create shares of its own stock. And if there are trades happening away from the company's knowledge, that's bad. And I don't share that intuition. And I'm with Vlad Tenev that, yeah, if you want to make your own AMC stock, essentially, these tokens are... First of all, Robinhood's tokens are backed by AMC stock. Robinhood buys the stock and then sells tokens representing that stock to foreign investors because security is law. The U.S. implications are not, like, entirely settled yet, and so they just do this abroad. But so, like, they're not exactly creating AMC stock, but they could. They could. Like, you could sell forwards. Like, I've written about this a lot because, like, there's a lot of this stuff happening with private stocks, right? Like, AMC is a public company. They're mad about it. Like, the things they're mad about are slightly different from, like, the things Anthropic is mad about or things, you know. Before it went public, SpaceX was getting tokenized by Robinhood and Elon Musk was mad about it. And like there, you know, those companies were like, we're private companies. We really should be able to control our shareholder base. And so when people were selling forwards on them or like plopping their shares into SPVs and selling SPV shares, the companies would get mad. With a public company, it's like you do have less control, but still like there's this long history of meme stock companies getting very nervous about short sellers and phantom shares and like, You know, not knowing where their shares are and like telling their shareholders to recall their shares from street name and own them directly so that they could have a direct relationship with their shareholders.
turns.zh: 而且，我不知道。我写这篇的时候是这么想的：有一种非常强烈的直觉，尤其是在 meme 股公司那里——不知为何，也确实有道理——就是：只有一家公司才能创造自己股票的股份。如果有交易是在公司不知情的情况下发生的，那就是坏事。我并不认同这种直觉。在这点上我站 Vlad Tenev：是啊，如果你想自己造一种 AMC 股票，本质上这些代币是……首先，Robinhood 的代币是有 AMC 股票作支撑的。Robinhood 买进股票，然后把代表这些股票的代币卖给外国投资者，因为'证券即法律'（security is law）。在美国的法律影响还没完全定论，所以他们就在海外做这件事。所以说，他们并不完全是凭空创造 AMC 股票，但他们可以，他们真能这么做。比如你可以卖出远期合约（forwards）。这个话题我写过很多，因为私有股票那边正发生着大量这类事情，对吧？AMC 是一家上市公司。他们为此生气。而他们生气的点，跟 Anthropic 生气的点、或者跟 SpaceX 的略有不同——在 SpaceX 上市之前，Robinhood 就把它的股票代币化了，Elon Musk 为此很生气。那些公司当时说，我们是私有公司，我们理应能掌控自己的股东基础。所以当有人卖出它们的远期合约，或者把它们的股份塞进 SPV、再卖 SPV 的份额时，这些公司就会火大。而对一家上市公司来说，你的掌控力确实更小，但仍然有很长的历史：meme 股公司对空头（short sellers）、幽灵股份（phantom shares）非常紧张，担心不知道自己的股票都在哪儿，还会叫股东把股票从'街名'（street name）里召回、直接持有，好让公司能跟股东建立直接关系。

turns.en: Matt, when I was a wee lad, one of my first interviews ever of all time as a finance reporter was with the overstock.com people.
turns.zh: Matt，我当年还是个小年轻的时候，我做金融记者最早的几次采访之一，就是采访 Overstock.com 的人。

turns.en: Oh.
turns.zh: 哦。

turns.en: And they were so upset about insider trading naked.
turns.zh: 他们对裸……内幕交易（insider trading）气得不行。

turns.en: Naked short selling. Yeah.
turns.zh: 裸卖空（naked short selling）。对。

turns.en: Oh, pardon, pardon. I said insider trading.
turns.zh: 哦，抱歉抱歉。我说成内幕交易了。

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没事儿。

turns.en: Naked short selling. Right. Talk my ear off about it.
turns.zh: 裸卖空。对。他们跟我絮叨了这个半天，说得我耳朵都起茧了。

turns.en: Yeah, no, I've written about the overstock.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错，我写过 Overstock 的事。

turns.en: That was a long time ago. But let's talk about another way of owning things. You can own a token, but I learned something in your column that I just simply did not know. So according to you, I really hope this is right. The entity that owns most shares of most companies is called Seed & Co., which sounds like something you would make up because it's spelled C-E-D-E.
turns.zh: 那是很久以前的事了。不过我们来聊聊另一种持有东西的方式。你可以持有一个代币，但我在你的专栏里学到一件我压根儿不知道的事。据你说——我真希望这是对的——持有大多数公司大部分股份的那个实体，叫 Cede & Co.，这名字听起来像是你编出来的，因为它拼作 C-E-D-E。

turns.en: But... No, this is true. Actually, I went and looked and Wikipedia quotes a report from 1998 saying that Seed & Co owns 83% of all stocks in the United States. That was a long time ago, but I do think it's roughly true. If you look at DTC, DTC is the depository trust company. It is what I usually think of as owning all of the stocks, although for reasons we can get to, it's actually Seed & Co. But DTC, which is the same as Seed & Co, DTC says that it has custody of about $ 74 trillion of equities, which is in round numbers, like half of the market cap of like the global equity market cap. But like DTC is pretty US centric. So like it's much more than half of US stocks. On the order of most companies, 80% of their stock is owned by Seed & Co, which is the nominee of DTC. There's a reason for that, which people have explained to me multiple times because I always forget.
turns.zh: 但……不，这是真的。我其实还去查了，Wikipedia 上引用了一份 1998 年的报告，说 Cede & Co. 持有美国所有股票的 83%。那是很久以前了，但我确实觉得这大致是真的。如果你看 DTC——DTC 就是存托信托公司（Depository Trust Company）——它通常是我脑海里那个'持有所有股票'的实体，尽管出于我们待会儿能讲到的原因，实际上是 Cede & Co.。但 DTC，跟 Cede & Co. 是一回事，DTC 说它托管着约 74 万亿美元的股票，取个整数的话，大约相当于全球股票总市值的一半。不过 DTC 是相当以美国为中心的，所以它占美股的比例远不止一半。对大多数公司来说，大约 80% 的股票由 Cede & Co. 持有，而 Cede & Co. 是 DTC 的代名人（nominee）。这是有原因的，人们跟我解释过好多次，因为我老是忘。

turns.en: Do you want to take a swing at it? Okay.
turns.zh: 你想试着讲讲吗？好。

turns.en: So the reason for that is that DTC is a corporation. And because of the need to transfer stocks quickly, they need one person to be able to do it. And so Seed & Co is some sort of partnership that one partner of Seed & Co can sign the transfer documents. And so it's the nominee for DTC. This may not be exactly right, but it's rough.
turns.zh: 原因在于，DTC 是一家公司（corporation）。而因为需要快速转让股票，他们需要有'一个人'能来办这件事。所以 Cede & Co. 是某种合伙企业（partnership），Cede & Co. 的一位合伙人就能签署转让文件。因此它是 DTC 的代名人。这可能不完全准确，但大致如此。

turns.en: I liked it.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个解释。

turns.en: Anyway, Seed & Co owns all the stocks. And so if you own stock through... Robinhood, you know, like what happens is that you own an entry on Robinhood's ledger saying that you own some stock and Robinhood owns an entry on DTC's ledger and Seed & Co has nominee for DTC owns stock on like AMC's ledger. And so most companies like don't directly have like a list of shareholders. It's not like the company keeps the list of shareholders. The company keeps a list of shareholders, but like the number one name on the list is Seed & Co and everyone who owns stock through a brokerage or in like normal ways owns through Seed & Co.
turns.zh: 总之，Cede & Co. 持有所有的股票。所以如果你通过……Robinhood 持有股票，情况是这样：你在 Robinhood 的账本上拥有一条记录，说你持有某些股票；Robinhood 在 DTC 的账本上拥有一条记录；而 Cede & Co.，作为 DTC 的代名人，在比如 AMC 的账本上持有股票。所以大多数公司并不直接持有一份股东名单。不是说公司不保存股东名单——公司确实保存一份股东名单，但名单上排在第一位的名字是 Cede & Co.，而所有通过券商、或以常规方式持股的人，都是通过 Cede & Co. 持有的。

turns.en: Including me.
turns.zh: 包括我。

turns.en: Potentially. Probably. And the reason for this is like in the olden days, if you wanted to buy stock, like I would give you money and you would give me a stock certificate. And this was an incredibly inefficient way to run a financial system. And so they were like, what if we just put all the stock certificates in one place? And instead of like moving them around, we just called it that one place and said like cross off Max's name and write my name on it, right? Oh, let's do it the other way around. Or whatever, yeah. And that's like the system that develops. So DTC is like the clearinghouse. It just has all the stocks. And it keeps track of the movements of the stock rather than relying on companies or transfer agents or like paper share certificates. But that was an incredibly efficiency enhancing development in like the 60s and 70s. And now people are like, there has to be a better way. So you hear like a lot of like, we'll put it on the blockchain, right? So the idea is that there should be a shareholder list that the company maintains or is maintained on the blockchain that doesn't involve this weird third party. And so this is a thing that comes up a lot. And one way it comes up is tokenization. When people say tokenization of stocks, they mean a lot of different things. But one thing they could mean is some sort of blockchain-based public ledger of each company's stock such that you didn't need to have any sort of intermediary like TTC or like Robinhood. And, like, AMC would just have its own, like, you know, perfect share ledger that everyone could sort of see and that it could have a direct relationship with the shareholders. But that's not what's happening here. What's happening here is that Robinhood is doing its own thing and, like, just issuing some sort of derivative security on a blockchain.
turns.zh: 有可能。多半是。原因在于，在过去，如果你想买股票，就是我给你钱、你给我一张股票凭证（stock certificate）。而这是运营一个金融系统极其低效的方式。于是他们就想，如果我们把所有的股票凭证都放在一个地方呢？与其把它们搬来搬去，不如直接给那个地方打个电话，说，把 Max 的名字划掉、写上我的名字，对吧？哦，反过来也行。诸如此类，是啊。这就是后来发展出来的系统。所以 DTC 就像是那个清算所（clearinghouse）。它就是持有所有的股票，跟踪股票的流转，而不再依赖公司、过户代理（transfer agents）或者纸质股票凭证。这在六七十年代是一项极大提升效率的发展。而现在人们又说，肯定有更好的办法。于是你会听到很多'把它放到区块链上'的说法，对吧？这个想法是：应该有一份由公司维护、或者在区块链上维护的股东名单，不涉及这个古怪的第三方。所以这个话题经常出现。它出现的一种方式就是代币化（tokenization）。当人们说'股票的代币化'时，他们指的是很多不同的东西。但其中一种可能指的是：某种基于区块链的、每家公司股票的公开账本，这样你就不需要 DTC 或 Robinhood 之类的任何中介。AMC 就会有它自己那份完美的股份账本，人人都能看到，它也能跟股东建立直接关系。但这里发生的并不是这个。这里发生的是，Robinhood 在做它自己的事，就是在区块链上发行某种衍生证券（derivative security）。

turns.en: You know, Seed & Company reminds me of. What? I'm a big fan of Seed & Company from here on in. It reminds me of, I think, the single funniest finance-related piece of humor. Not by you. Actually, I think possibly at the root of our work friendship. It's a Saturday Night Live skit, possibly from the late 80s, might be the early 90s. It's like a black and white ad for a very important investment bank. And it's like a really handsome old man. He's like, what we do at our company is we write down our clients. We put it on a piece of paper. And we keep that piece of paper.
turns.zh: 你知道，Cede & Co. 让我想起了……什么来着？从现在起我算是 Cede & Co. 的忠实粉丝了。它让我想起，我觉得，是最好笑的一段跟金融相关的幽默。不是你写的。其实我觉得，它可能正是我俩工作友谊的根源。那是《Saturday Night Live》的一个小品，可能是 80 年代末的，也可能是 90 年代初。它像是一支为一家非常重要的投资银行做的黑白广告。里面是个特别帅气的老先生。他说，我们公司的业务，就是把我们的客户写下来，写在一张纸上，然后把那张纸保存好。

turns.en: I'm blanking on the name. It's a famous one. It's one of two Jim Downey ads for Saturday Night Live. The other one is the Change Bank. But the, what's the name? Grayson Moorhead Security. Oh, good, Matt. I think is what it's called. And it's very funny. Like, the tagline is like, at Grayson Moorhead Trust Department, we will write down a list of our customers and we'll keep it in a safe place. If there is time, we will make a copy of the list.
turns.zh: 我一下想不起名字了。这是个很有名的段子。它是 Jim Downey 为《Saturday Night Live》做的两支广告之一。另一支是那个 Change Bank。不过，叫什么来着？Grayson Moorhead Security。哦，好，Matt，我想它就叫这个名字。它非常好笑。那句标语是：在 Grayson Moorhead 信托部，我们会把客户名单写下来，放在一个安全的地方。如果时间允许，我们还会把这份名单复印一份。

turns.en: In case something happens to the first list.
turns.zh: 以防第一份名单出什么岔子。

turns.en: I quote that ad sometimes because, like, I read about, like, complicated high finance and, like, There's like this baseline level of finance that is like a bank is in the business of keeping a list of who has money at the bank. And like most of the time that doesn't come up. It's not like in the news. It's just like a sort of background assumption. But sometimes it comes up. Sometimes they get the list wrong.
turns.zh: 我有时会引用那支广告，因为我读的是那些复杂的高端金融（high finance），而金融有一个基础层面，就是：银行的业务，就是保存一份'谁在银行里有钱'的名单。大多数时候这一点不会被提起，不会上新闻，它只是一个背景式的假设。但有时候它就会被提起。有时候他们还会把这份名单弄错。

turns.en: True mat heads, real money stuff fans will know that you love nothing more than an entry on a ledger.
turns.zh: 真正的 Matt 铁粉、真正的 Money Stuff 粉丝都会知道，你最喜欢的莫过于账本上的一条记录了。

turns.en: Oh, I love an entry on a ledger.
turns.zh: 哦，我太爱账本上的一条记录了。

turns.en: In fact, I believe you.
turns.zh: 说真的，我信你。

turns.en: This is why I wrote 50,000 words about crypto once.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么我曾经写过 5 万字讲加密货币（crypto）。

turns.en: Do you not define a dollar as like basically a one that's on the ledger somewhere?
turns.zh: 你不是把一美元基本定义成'某处账本上的一个 1'吗？

turns.en: I mean, yeah. That's what it is, right? A dollar is an entry on a ledger at a bank.
turns.zh: 我是说，对。它就是这个，对吧？一美元就是银行账本上的一条记录。

turns.en: And it's just so satisfying to think that there's a room with pieces of paper somewhere, you know?
turns.zh: 想到某个地方有一个房间，里面堆着一张张纸，这真是太让人满足了，你懂吧？

turns.en: No, there's not really. It's a computer.
turns.zh: 不，其实并没有。那是一台电脑。

turns.en: I insist. I insist on it. Quick shout out to 1995.
turns.zh: 我坚持。我就要坚持这一点。顺便快速致敬一下 1995 年。

turns.en: Oh, by the way, when you say a room with pieces of paper, so like one thing about Seed & Co, like the normal way to think about how stocks are owned is that the company has an electronic list of its shareholders, which is maintained by a service provider called the transfer agent. And on that electronic list, it lists its shareholders, and most of the shareholders are Seed & Co. Like Seed & Co owns 80% of the stock, and then Seed & Co keeps its own list. And so these are all electronic entries. But in the not that, I mean, 20, 30 years ago, a lot of stuff was share certificates. And a lot of what DTC, the depository, did was, like, have vaults with share certificates. And then it would have an electronic list of who owned the shares. But, like, the underlying shares consisted in paper form at their vault, which flooded in a hurricane.
turns.zh: 哦，顺便说一句，你说到'一个堆着纸的房间'，关于 Cede & Co. 有一点：通常理解股票如何被持有的方式是，公司有一份电子股东名单，由一家叫过户代理（transfer agent）的服务商维护。在那份电子名单上，列着它的股东，而大多数股东就是 Cede & Co.。比如 Cede & Co. 持有 80% 的股票，然后 Cede & Co. 自己再保存一份名单。所以这些都是电子记录。但在——我是说，二三十年前——很多东西还是纸质股票凭证。DTC，也就是那个存托机构，做的很多事，就是设一些金库来存放股票凭证。然后它会有一份电子名单，记录谁持有这些股份。但底层的股份是以纸质形式存放在他们的金库里的，而那个金库在一场飓风中被淹了。

turns.en: Really?
turns.zh: 真的假的？

turns.en: Yeah. Anyway, also, I've written about this, but a guy wrote a novel called The Vault, which is about, like, someone doing a heist at the DTC, which is, like, again, like, Not a real thing. They're not all bear security. But it's a good concept for a novel.
turns.zh: 是啊。总之，还有，这个我写过，有个人写了本小说叫《The Vault》，讲的是有人去 DTC 打劫，而这，同样，也不是真事儿。它们并不都是无记名证券（bearer security）。但作为小说的构思，这挺不错。

turns.en: You know, someone on Twitter started posting individual frames of Heat, the 1995 Michael Mann classic. And I found out my wife had never seen it. So this week I rewatched it. And there is not merely a subplot. I mean, in a way, it's crucial to the movie that they steal bear bones.
turns.zh: 你知道，Twitter 上有人开始一帧一帧地发《Heat》——那部 1995 年 Michael Mann 的经典——的画面。结果我发现我老婆从没看过它。所以这周我重看了一遍。而片子里不只是一条支线剧情，我是说，某种意义上，'他们偷无记名债券（bearer bonds）'这件事对整部电影至关重要。

turns.en: Sure. It's crucial in every movie.
turns.zh: 当然。它在每部电影里都至关重要。

turns.en: And what a good scene that is.
turns.zh: 而那场面多棒啊。

turns.en: Diehard, too, right? Like, Bearer Bonds.
turns.zh: 《Die Hard》里也有，对吧？就是无记名债券。

turns.en: Oh, it is also Diehard.
turns.zh: 哦，《Die Hard》里也确实有。

turns.en: Bearer Bonds, big thing.
turns.zh: 无记名债券，可是个大东西。

turns.en: Bearer Bonds are the heart and soul of American cinema, post-1980.
turns.zh: 无记名债券是 1980 年以后美国电影的灵魂所在。

turns.en: Yes, and by the time they were a big cinematic trip, they were not really a financial thing anymore.
turns.zh: 是的，而且等到它们在电影里大出风头的时候，它们在金融上其实已经不算什么了。

turns.en: I've never heard of them. I only know about Bearer Bonds. That's a heat. What's the concern?
turns.zh: 我以前从没听说过它们。我只知道《Heat》里的无记名债券。那都是《Heat》里的，有什么好担心的？

turns.en: Did you talk about Apollo?
turns.zh: 你要聊聊 Apollo 吗？

turns.en: I do want to talk about Apollo.
turns.zh: 我确实想聊聊 Apollo。

turns.en: So there's this paper finding that it's measuring how much private equity firms, portfolio companies pay to borrow money. And they say, We find that under three measures of reputation, portfolio companies owned by the most aggressive sponsors pay considerably higher yields than those owned by more genial sponsors. I really like the idea of genial sponsors. I really like my like sort of paradigm of like the private equity industry is that is not a fun interest. Whatever. It has its perks, but like, it's not like a genial industry. It's not like, you know, it's not like people sitting around and being like, oh, it's so nice to work here. It's like, you know, it's kind of tough. And then like, There is in this paper a league table of, I think I called it, I called it the league table of sponsor aggressiveness. But you could call it the league table of sponsor geniality.
turns.zh: 有这么一篇论文，它衡量的是私募股权（private equity）公司旗下的组合公司借钱要付多少利息。他们说：'我们发现，在三种声誉衡量标准下，由最激进的保荐方（sponsors）持有的组合公司，支付的收益率明显高于由更和善（genial）的保荐方持有的公司。'我特别喜欢'和善的保荐方'这个说法。我对私募股权行业的这种基本认知是：它不是一个'和善'的行业。随你怎么说。它有它的好处，但它不是一个和善的行业。它不是那种，你知道，人们围坐在一起说'哦，在这儿干活真好'的行业。它是……有点残酷的。然后这篇论文里有一个排行榜（league table），我记得我叫它'保荐方激进度排行榜'。但你也可以叫它'保荐方和善度排行榜'。

turns.en: Depending on which one was top. You know, I was so mad at you and so disappointed when I went to, what's it called, like SSSN or something like that?
turns.zh: 就看哪个排在榜首了。你知道，我对你又气又失望，当时我跑去那个叫什么来着，SSSN 之类的地方？

turns.en: SSRN. Uh-huh.
turns.zh: SSRN。嗯哼。

turns.en: And I downloaded the paper.
turns.zh: 然后我下载了那篇论文。

turns.en: You searched for the phrase league table.
turns.zh: 你搜了'league table'这个词组。

turns.en: And it was not there, and I thought, that rascal.
turns.zh: 结果它根本不在里面，我就想，这个狡猾的家伙。

turns.en: I made up that name. But no, they have a list of like 25 private equity firms ranked in order of aggressiveness. And the ranking is very strange. It's like, as I said, the three measures of reputation. So one is they went to ChatGPT and Claude and were like, what's the most aggressive private equity firms? And they had the LLMs rank them. And the LLMs drew on accumulated human knowledge to be like, Apollo's the most aggressive.
turns.zh: 那个名字是我编的。不过不是，他们有一份大约 25 家私募股权公司的名单，按激进度排序。而这个排序非常奇怪。就像我说的，有三种声誉衡量方式。其中一种是，他们跑去问 ChatGPT 和 Claude：最激进的私募股权公司是哪些？然后让这些大语言模型（LLM）来排序。而这些 LLM 调用积累下来的人类知识，给出的答案是：Apollo 最激进。

turns.en: Sorry, that's real?
turns.zh: 抱歉，这是真的？

turns.en: That's what they did? That's really what they did. That's one of the three methods.
turns.zh: 他们就是这么干的？他们真的就是这么干的。这是三种方法之一。

turns.en: That's also disappointing.
turns.zh: 这也挺让人失望的。

turns.en: Yeah. That's one of their methods. Another method is they just looked at which sponsors had done the phrase is liability management exercises, basically like quasi-coercive debt exchanges where like, you know, you extract some money from creditors to give to other creditors. And if you did an LME, you were in the more aggressive bucket. And if you didn't do an LME, you're in the less aggressive bucket. And the third measure of reputation, the third measure is that they put the sponsors into two buckets. One was Apollo because they just thought of Apollo as having the most aggressive reputation. And the other was the other 24 sponsors. And they said like, Apollo, because it is sort of known as the most aggressive sponsor at extracting value from creditors, it was just, they did a regression with Apollo in one bucket and the other sponsors in the other. And they found that the most aggressive sponsors pay higher yields than those owned by more genial sponsors. And they found that Apollo loans in particular carry a premium of about 100 basis points compared to other sponsors.
turns.zh: 是啊。这是他们的方法之一。另一种方法是，他们直接看哪些保荐方做过——这个说法叫'负债管理操作'（liability management exercises，LME）——基本上就是那种准强制性的债务置换，你从一些债权人那里榨出钱来给另一些债权人。如果你做过 LME，你就被归到更激进的那一档；如果没做过，你就在没那么激进的那一档。而第三种声誉衡量方式是，他们把保荐方分成两档：一档是 Apollo，因为他们就是觉得 Apollo 的声誉最激进；另一档是其余 24 家保荐方。他们说，Apollo 因为在从债权人身上榨取价值方面算是公认最激进的保荐方，所以……他们就是做了一个回归，把 Apollo 放一档、其他保荐方放另一档。结果发现，最激进的保荐方支付的收益率高于由更和善的保荐方持有的公司。而且他们发现，尤其是 Apollo 的贷款，相比其他保荐方，带有大约 100 个基点（basis points）的溢价。

turns.en: I'm sorry, that's like real money at the end of the day, right? Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 抱歉，说到底那可是真金白银，对吧？哦，是的。

turns.en: I mean, like, 100 basis points, you know, spread on a sample where, like, the average thing yields 717 basis points.
turns.zh: 我是说，100 个基点，你知道，是在一个平均收益率 717 个基点的样本上的利差。

turns.en: That's like a jerk premium?
turns.zh: 这算不算是'混蛋溢价'（jerk premium）？

turns.en: Well, so what I wrote about this is, like, so, like, Apollo would dispute this, but, like, yeah, I think it's fair to characterize it as a jerk premium.
turns.zh: 嗯，我写这件事的时候是这么说的：Apollo 会对此有异议，但，是啊，我觉得把它形容成'混蛋溢价'是说得过去的。

turns.en: Or let's not even say jerk. Let's just say aggressiveness premium.
turns.zh: 或者我们连'混蛋'都别说了。就说'激进度溢价'吧。

turns.en: Yeah, but, like, what is aggressiveness? Like, what I wrote is, like, I don't think it's, um, it's not like a moral premium. It's not like people are mad, and so they're like, ah, you have to pay more because I'm mad. It's saying, look, we know that Apollo has this reputation for extracting value from creditors. We're a creditor. We don't want value extracted from us, but we expect them to extract value from us. That's why, you know, that's what they do. And if we expect them to extract value from us, we have to charge them for that upfront. And so we charge them an extra hundred basis points. That's kind of like the way to model it. Now, again, like you can dispute the facts, right? Like Apollo says, this is a flawed methodology. And like, it's like one or two transactions years ago, it doesn't, but they're not wrong that there is a certain reputation for aggressiveness. And then the question is, if Apollo is paying 100 basis points a year for that reputation, is it getting its money's worth, right? And if, in fact, they continue to extract value from creditors, then maybe 100 basis points a year is a perfectly fine price to pay for that.
turns.zh: 是啊，但，什么是'激进'呢？我写的是，我不觉得它是一种……它不是一种道德溢价。不是说人们生气了，所以就说'啊，因为我在气头上，你得多付钱'。它的意思是：听着，我们知道 Apollo 有这个从债权人身上榨取价值的声誉。我们是债权人。我们不想被榨取价值，但我们预期他们会从我们身上榨取价值。这就是……你知道，这就是他们的做派。而如果我们预期他们会榨取我们的价值，我们就得为此预先向他们收费。所以我们就多收他们 100 个基点。这大概就是给这件事建模的方式。当然，你还是可以对事实提出异议，对吧？Apollo 说，这是一套有缺陷的方法论，而且那不过是多年前的一两笔交易，说明不了什么——但他们说'确实存在某种激进的声誉'这一点并没有错。那么问题就是：如果 Apollo 每年为这个声誉付出 100 个基点，它花得值不值？如果事实上他们持续从债权人身上榨取价值，那么每年 100 个基点也许是个完全划算的价钱。

turns.en: How lucrative is their aggressiveness? Right.
turns.zh: 他们的激进到底有多赚钱？对吧。

turns.en: And the paper sadly does not measure that. And again, Apollo's like, oh, it was years ago. So they're not like, yes, we're going to ruthlessly... fleece our creditors tomorrow, right? But it's like, you know, there's some chance that, like, on balance, Apollo makes more for its equity investors even after accounting for the extra 100 basis points of alleged yield spread.
turns.zh: 可惜的是，这篇论文并没有衡量这一点。而且，Apollo 又会说，哦，那是多年前的事了。所以他们并不是那种'是的，我们明天就要无情地……狠狠薅我们债权人羊毛'的做派，对吧？但这就像，你知道，有可能总体而言，即便算上那多出来的、被指称的 100 个基点收益率利差，Apollo 为它的股权投资者赚的钱还是更多。

turns.en: You know, on, like, a personal basis, no one would, I guess, want to be called aggressive.
turns.zh: 你知道，就个人层面来说，我猜没人愿意被人说'激进'。

turns.en: Oh, I disagree.
turns.zh: 哦，我不同意。

turns.en: But what I was just going to say, I was just going to say, in finance, though, what an incredible compliment to their minds.
turns.zh: 但我刚要说的是，我正要说的，不过话说回来，在金融圈，被人说激进可是了不起的恭维。

turns.en: So, again, like, Apollo's like, oh, that's not true. But, like, let's say they just embrace it, right? And they go out to raise money for their private equity funds. And they go to a private equity limited partner and they say, invest in our fund. It's great. And the private equity LP is like, well, I don't know. These other sponsors are paying less for debt. And so that's going to eat into my returns. And then Apollo's like, it's because we're aggressive. Of course you want to be with the aggressive one. Of course you want the people who are going to maximize. When people discuss private equity aggressiveness, at some point someone always says, look, we're fiduciaries for pension funds, whatever. We're fiduciaries for our clients. And so we're not being aggressive. We're just being zealous in, you know, maximizing returns for our clients. And here's like outside evidence of that, right? Here's someone being like, wow, Apollo is really zealous in maximizing value for their, you know, private equity clients, right? It's a good advertisement.
turns.zh: 所以，同样，Apollo 会说，哦，那不是真的。但，比方说他们干脆就认下这一点，对吧？他们出去为旗下的私募股权基金募资，找到一位私募股权的有限合伙人（limited partner，LP），说，投资我们的基金吧，它很棒。而那位 LP 说，嗯，我不确定。别的保荐方借钱付的利息更少，那会吃掉我的回报。然后 Apollo 就说，那是因为我们激进。你当然想跟激进的那家在一起。你当然想要那种会把回报最大化的人。当人们讨论私募股权的激进度时，总有某个时刻会有人说：听着，我们是养老基金之类的受托人（fiduciaries），我们是客户的受托人。所以我们并不是激进，我们只是热心于为客户实现回报最大化。而这里就有一份来自外部的证据，对吧？有人站出来说，哇，Apollo 在为其私募股权客户实现价值最大化方面真的很卖力，对吧？这是很好的广告。

turns.en: It's a delightful compliment.
turns.zh: 这是一句很妙的恭维。

turns.en: Now, again, like there's a weirdness here, which is that Apollo now runs much more debt than equity, right? And like, are kind of trying to move away from their reputation for aggressiveness. And so they can't just be like, yeah, we're aggressive, whatever. But like, you know, I would be.
turns.zh: 不过话说回来，这里有个别扭之处：Apollo 现在管的债务（debt）远多于股权（equity），对吧？而且他们多少在试图摆脱那个'激进'的声誉。所以他们没法干脆地说'是啊，我们就激进，怎么了'。但，你知道，换我我就会这么说。

turns.en: You know, how I knew it was going to be a good item. It includes the line in money stuff. Ooh, these guys are good at extracting money from creditors exposed. So we're going to charge them for that ex ante, which has three key signs of a good mat line.
turns.zh: 你知道，我怎么就知道这会是个好条目。它里面有 Money Stuff 的那句话：'Ooh，这帮人擅长从债权人身上榨钱，所以我们要事先（ex ante）就为这个向他们收费。'这句话具备一句好的 Matt 金句的三大关键标志。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: It's got a little bit of Latin.
turns.zh: 它带一点拉丁文。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: I believe you are classics. It's got the word.
turns.zh: 我记得你是学古典学的。它还带着那个词。

turns.en: Ooh, which is, I love saying ooh.
turns.zh: Ooh，那个词是——我特别爱说 ooh。

turns.en: You love saying ooh. A key word I would like to say on a personal note. A key word in my wife's vows to me.
turns.zh: 你爱说 ooh。有个词我想说句私人的话——那是我妻子对我立下的誓言里的一个关键词。

turns.en: Ooh.
turns.zh: Ooh。

turns.en: The word ooh is so close to my heart as well, Matt. And then it also has.
turns.zh: ooh 这个词也让我倍感亲切，Matt。然后它还带着……

turns.en: Are you going to say the line?
turns.zh: 你打算把那句话念出来吗？

turns.en: Do you want to hear it?
turns.zh: 你想听吗？

turns.en: Yeah, sure.
turns.zh: 想啊，当然。

turns.en: It's actually very moving.
turns.zh: 它其实很打动人。

turns.en: Okay. I think... In the middle of a sentence. We'll get to your third item in the sentence in a bit.
turns.zh: 好。我想……'在一句话的中间'。我们待会儿再回到你那第三个'一句话里的标志'。

turns.en: In the middle of a sentence. The line, at least according to the laws in our vows, is that Anne Bancroft said of Mel Brooks, her husband, every time I hear his key in the door, it's like, ooh, there's a party that's going to start.
turns.zh: '在一句话的中间'。那句话——至少按我们誓言里的说法——是 Anne Bancroft 形容她丈夫 Mel Brooks 的：'每次我听到他的钥匙插进门里，那感觉就像，ooh，一场派对要开始了。'

turns.en: Aw, that's so nice.
turns.zh: 哇，真好。

turns.en: Yeah, it really is lovely.
turns.zh: 是啊，真的很美好。

turns.en: Also a good description of Max Abelson.
turns.zh: 这也是对 Max Abelson 的绝佳形容。

turns.en: Oh, Matt, that's so sweet. And now I need to finish my compliment of your one line. And this one's important. Not just Latin, not just the word ooh. But imagine dialogue.
turns.zh: 哦，Matt，太甜了。现在我得把对你那句话的恭维讲完。而这一点很重要：不只是拉丁文，不只是 ooh 这个词，而是要想象成对话。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: I think I told you very early in our relationship. It's simply my favorite thing in money stuff.
turns.zh: 我想我在我们认识很早就跟你说过。它简直就是我在 Money Stuff 里最喜欢的东西。

turns.en: It is an important component of money stuff.
turns.zh: 它确实是 Money Stuff 的一个重要组成部分。

turns.en: It's key.
turns.zh: 它是关键。

turns.en: It's usually about Elon Musk, but not always.
turns.zh: 它通常是关于 Elon Musk 的，但也不总是。

turns.en: Sometimes.
turns.zh: 有时候。

turns.en: Wait, ooh, ooh, I do feel like comes from my desk at Goldman, actually. Like, I feel like there's... Is that true? Yeah, yeah. Like, when we were, like, sarcastically describing things, we were like, ooh.
turns.zh: 等等，ooh、ooh，我确实觉得这个说法源自我在 Goldman 的那个交易台。我感觉那儿……是真的吗？是啊是啊。就是当我们带着讽刺去描述某些事情时，我们会说，ooh。

turns.en: They're like, ooh, a party's about to start.
turns.zh: 他们就像在说，ooh，一场派对要开始了。

turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 正是。

turns.en: You know, I searched ooh and money stuff.
turns.zh: 你知道，我在 Money Stuff 里搜了 ooh。

turns.en: I think there's a lot.
turns.zh: 我记得有很多。

turns.en: Dozens.
turns.zh: 好几十个。

turns.en: Dozens?
turns.zh: 几十个？

turns.en: And I'm telling you right now.
turns.zh: 我现在就告诉你。

turns.en: So many columns. I would have said hundreds, but okay.
turns.zh: 那么多专栏里都有。我本来会说有好几百个，不过行吧。

turns.en: Oh, I think it was like, I don't know because I'm going to say like 112. Okay, okay.
turns.zh: 哦，我记得好像是，我不确定，因为我要说是大概 112 个。好，好。

turns.en: 112 oohs.
turns.zh: 112 个 ooh。

turns.en: Ooh is such a better word than oh.
turns.zh: ooh 这个词可比 oh 好太多了。

turns.en: Well, it depends. They're different things.
turns.zh: 嗯，那得看情况。它们是不同的东西。

turns.en: No, it doesn't depend at all. Your average sentence with the word oh, like O-H obviously, average sentence with O-O-H, or even if you want O-H-H, it's going to be a better sentence.
turns.zh: 不，根本不看情况。一句普通的话里带上 oh 这个词，就是 O-H；而一句普通的话里带上 O-O-H，甚至你想用 O-H-H，那它都会是更好的一句话。

turns.en: O-H-H doesn't do much for me. Ooh, yeah, no, I agree that ooh, an ooh sentence is a better sentence than an oh sentence, but that's only, like, you know, you can't improve it just by swapping the oh for the ooh. You need to have the underlying ooh.
turns.zh: O-H-H 对我没什么吸引力。Ooh，是啊，不，我同意，一句带 ooh 的话比一句带 oh 的话更好，但那只是……你知道，你不能光靠把 oh 换成 ooh 就把句子变好。你得有那个底层的、名副其实的 ooh。

turns.en: Oh, you're saying?
turns.zh: 哦，你是说……？

turns.en: The substance needs to justify an ooh.
turns.zh: 内容本身得配得上一个 ooh。

turns.en: You're saying that the other words in the sentence besides the ooh also have to be good in order for the sentence to be good?
turns.zh: 你是说，一句话里除了 ooh 之外的其他词也得是好的，这句话才能算是好话？

turns.en: No, I'm saying that the ooh has to be contextually appropriate. Yeah, I agree. You can't just replace oh with ooh. They mean different things. Mmm, yeah.
turns.zh: 不，我是说这个 ooh 得在语境上合适。是啊，我同意。你不能光把 oh 替换成 ooh。它们意思不一样。嗯，对。

turns.en: They mean different things. I guess I can agree on that.
turns.zh: 它们意思不一样。这一点我大概能同意。

turns.en: Wait, oh, these guys are good at extracting value. Ooh, these guys are good at extracting value. Very different meanings. And that was the Money Stuff Podcast. I'm Matt Levine.
turns.zh: 等等，'oh，这帮人擅长榨取价值'，跟'ooh，这帮人擅长榨取价值'，意思非常不同。好了，以上就是本期 Money Stuff 播客。我是 Matt Levine。

turns.zh: 我是 Max Abelson。
